headline: YouTube May Be Hiding the Dislike Button

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: YouTube is a website where people watch videos. Under each video, there are two buttons: one for "like" and one for "dislike." The dislike button lets people say they did not enjoy a video. Now, YouTube might be testing a change. Some people noticed that the dislike button is moving to a hidden menu. This menu has three dots, and you have to click it to find more choices. If the dislike button is harder to find, fewer people will probably use it. This is not new for YouTube. In 2021, YouTube already hid the number of dislikes a video gets, so only the people who made the video can see that number. This was meant to protect video creators from mean comments. YouTube also removed the dislike button from short videos called Shorts earlier this year. Nobody knows yet if this new change will happen for everyone. YouTube has not said anything about it yet. People who use YouTube a lot are watching closely to see what happens next.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: YouTube seems to be testing a change that would make the dislike button harder to find. Right now, when you watch a video, the like and dislike buttons sit side by side, making it quick and easy to react to a video. But some users have noticed that the dislike button is being moved into a smaller menu, marked by three dots, that you have to click open first. If this change becomes permanent, it would take more steps to dislike a video, and that extra effort would likely mean fewer people bother to do it. This matters because dislikes help show how people really feel about a video, and creators use that feedback to understand their audience. This isn't the first time YouTube has changed how dislikes work. Back in 2021, the company stopped showing the public dislike count, meaning viewers can no longer see how many people disliked a video, even though creators can still see that number themselves. YouTube said this was done to protect creators from being targeted or harassed by groups of people who dislike videos just to be mean. Earlier this year, YouTube also removed the dislike button entirely from YouTube Shorts, its short-video feature, encouraging people to use other options in the three-dot menu instead. It's still unclear how many people are seeing this new test or whether YouTube plans to roll it out to everyone. The company has not yet responded to questions about it. This shows that YouTube keeps experimenting with how people can express their opinions about videos.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: YouTube appears to be testing a feature that would hide the dislike button on videos, based on reports from tech news sites and users who have spotted the change. Normally, the like and dislike buttons appear right next to each other below a video, making it simple to react with one click. But some users on social media platforms like X (formerly Twitter) and Reddit have shared screenshots showing the dislike button tucked away inside a secondary menu, marked by three dots, instead of being visible right away. If this becomes a permanent change, interacting with the dislike button would require extra steps, and research on user behavior suggests that when something requires more effort, fewer people actually do it. This means dislikes could become much rarer, which could change how creators and viewers understand feedback on videos. This isn't a brand-new direction for YouTube. In 2021, the platform stopped publicly displaying the dislike count on videos, though creators can still view their own dislike numbers privately. YouTube explained this decision as a way to protect creators from harassment campaigns, where large groups sometimes dislike a video simply to bring down its numbers or pressure the creator, rather than because they disliked the actual content. Earlier this year, YouTube also eliminated the dislike button altogether from YouTube Shorts, its short-form video feature that competes with apps like TikTok and Instagram Reels, instead directing users toward other options tucked in the three-dot menu. It remains unclear how widespread this current test is or whether YouTube intends to apply the change to all users in the future. Google, YouTube's parent company, has not responded to requests for comment about the test. This situation highlights an ongoing tension for YouTube: balancing creators' desire for protection from unfair criticism or harassment with viewers' desire for honest, visible feedback about video quality. As YouTube continues to adjust how people can express approval or disapproval of content, both creators and viewers are left to wonder how these changes might reshape the platform's culture of feedback over time.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: YouTube appears to be quietly experimenting with hiding the dislike button, according to reporting from 9to5Google and observations shared by users across social media. Currently, the like and dislike buttons sit side by side beneath a video, allowing viewers to react with a single click. However, recent screenshots posted on X and Reddit show the dislike button relocated into a secondary "three-dot" menu, a less visible spot that requires an extra click to access. If this test becomes a permanent feature, the added friction could meaningfully reduce how often people use the dislike button, since behavioral research consistently shows that even small increases in effort can significantly lower how often people take an action. For creators, viewers, and the platform itself, this raises questions about what the dislike button is really for and whether YouTube is prioritizing creator comfort over transparent audience feedback. This potential change follows a pattern of YouTube gradually scaling back the visibility and influence of dislikes. In 2021, the platform removed the publicly visible dislike count from videos, meaning viewers can no longer see exactly how many people disliked a video, even though creators retain private access to that number through their analytics dashboard. YouTube justified that decision at the time as a way to shield creators from coordinated harassment campaigns, in which groups of users mass-dislike a video not because of its actual content but to punish or pressure a creator, sometimes for reasons unrelated to the video itself. More recently, earlier this year, YouTube removed the dislike button entirely from YouTube Shorts, its short-form video feature designed to compete with platforms like TikTok and Instagram Reels, pointing users instead toward alternative actions available in the three-dot menu. Together, these moves suggest a broader strategic shift at YouTube away from blunt, easily visible negative feedback tools and toward more private or buried alternatives. It remains unclear how widely this current test has been rolled out or whether YouTube plans to implement it platform-wide. Google, YouTube's parent company, did not immediately respond to a request for comment, leaving open questions about the company's intentions and timeline. For millions of creators who rely on audience feedback to shape their content, and for viewers who use dislikes to signal which videos are misleading, low-quality, or unhelpful, this change could meaningfully alter how trust and quality are communicated on one of the world's largest video platforms. It also raises a broader question relevant beyond YouTube: how should online platforms balance protecting creators from harassment with preserving honest, visible mechanisms for audience feedback?

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: YouTube appears to be testing a design change that would hide the dislike button from its default, easily accessible position beneath videos, according to reporting from 9to5Google and corroborating evidence shared by users on social media. Under the platform's current design, the like and dislike buttons appear side by side, allowing viewers to register a reaction with minimal effort. Recent screenshots posted on X and Reddit, however, show the dislike button relocated into a secondary "three-dot" overflow menu, a significantly less prominent location that requires an additional click to locate and use. If this experimental change is implemented broadly, the added interaction cost could substantially reduce engagement with the dislike function, since user-experience research has long demonstrated that even minor increases in the number of steps required to complete an action tend to suppress how often users bother to complete it at all. This raises deeper questions about the purpose dislikes serve on the platform and whether YouTube is increasingly prioritizing creator protection over transparent, easily accessible audience feedback mechanisms. This potential move fits into a broader, multi-year pattern of YouTube de-emphasizing the dislike feature. In 2021, the company eliminated the public display of dislike counts, meaning ordinary viewers can no longer see how many people disliked a given video, although creators retain private access to that figure through YouTube's analytics tools. At the time, YouTube framed this decision as a protective measure against coordinated harassment campaigns, in which organized groups of users would mass-dislike a video not necessarily because of dissatisfaction with its content, but as a form of targeted pressure or retaliation against a creator. More recently, earlier this year, YouTube removed the dislike button altogether from YouTube Shorts, its short-form video product built to compete directly with TikTok and Instagram Reels, instead steering users toward alternative engagement options buried within the three-dot menu. Viewed together, these incremental changes suggest a deliberate strategic direction: moving away from blunt, highly visible negative-feedback tools in favor of more private, harder-to-access alternatives that minimize public criticism of creators. It remains uncertain how widely this latest test has been deployed, whether it will be rolled out universally, or what timeline YouTube might follow, and Google, YouTube's parent company, did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding its intentions. For the millions of creators who depend on viewer feedback to refine and improve their content, and for audiences who rely on dislikes as a quick signal of a video's quality, accuracy, or usefulness, this change could meaningfully reshape how feedback functions on one of the world's most influential media platforms. More broadly, this episode reflects a recurring tension faced by large online platforms: the need to shield individual creators from harassment and abuse must be weighed against the broader public interest in maintaining honest, visible, and easily accessible tools for expressing disapproval or criticism.

questions: Do you think it's fair for YouTube to make it harder to dislike a video, or should viewers always have an easy way to share negative feedback?
How might hiding the dislike button change the way creators and audiences trust the videos they watch, at school or in everyday life?
Can you think of other situations, like at school or on other apps you use, where protecting someone from criticism might also hide useful information from others?
